deep.reconstruction:
Overall: the page is inverted relative to the archival foliation and mixes three things. (a) A list of mythological names for new planets. (b) Planetary-symbol doodles. (c) A short computation in Gauss's Theoria-Motus style coordinates. The tie to the discovery of Hebe, Iris and Flora (1847) and the '47' on the page suggest c. 1847 rather than 1824. This dating is my inference.

(1) Basic equation. For each of two bodies, let r = p/(1 - e cos(psi+theta)), where psi is an angle in the orbit (argument of latitude or true anomaly up to a constant). Write the rectangular coordinates as x = r*m*cos(psi+mu) and y = r*n*cos(psi+nu), with the parameter p absorbed into m and n. These are the Gaussian constants x = r sin a sin(A+u), recast with cosines. Primed letters belong to the second body.
Gauss writes
tang A = [m cos(psi+mu)/(1-e cos(psi+theta)) - m' cos(psi'+mu')/(1-e' cos(psi'+theta'))] / [n cos(psi+nu)/(1-e cos(psi+theta)) - n' cos(psi'+nu')/(1-e' cos(psi'+theta'))].
This says tan A = (x - x')/(y - y'). So A is the direction (e.g. longitude) of the line joining the two bodies, i.e. the position of one as seen from the other (geocentric longitude if the primed body is the Earth). The problem: given A, find the corresponding pairs (psi, psi'), i.e. when or where the relative direction takes a prescribed value.

(2) Clearing denominators.
As a model, Gauss first expands m cos(psi+mu)(1 - e' cos(psi'+theta')) - m' cos(psi'+mu')(1 - e cos(psi+theta)), the numerator x - x' times the denominators. Put c = cos psi, s = sin psi, c' = cos psi', s' = sin psi'. Then
m cos mu*c - m sin mu*s - m' cos mu'*c' + m' sin mu'*s' + (bilinear terms).
The cc' coefficient is -(m cos mu*e' cos theta' - m' cos mu'*e cos theta), exactly as written. He then tabulates which monomials occur (h, c, s, cc', cs', sc', ss'). The marginal note 'h, c, s, cc, cs = s'(h, c, s)' records the key structural fact: the equation has the form
P(c,s) + Q(c,s)*c' + R(c,s)*s' = 0, with P, Q, R linear in (1, c, s).
It is therefore linear in (c', s'). Combined with c'^2 + s'^2 = 1 this eliminates psi' and leaves a quartic in tan(psi/2). That last step is my completion; it is not on the page.
The full equation with tan A works the same way, with m cos(.+mu) replaced by m cos(.+mu) - tanA*n cos(.+nu), and similarly for the primed terms.

(3) Circular case e = e' = 0.
The condition becomes
m cos(psi+mu) - m' cos(psi'+mu') = tanA [n cos(psi+nu) - n' cos(psi'+nu')],
i.e.
(m cos mu - n tanA cos nu) c - (m sin mu - n tanA sin nu) s = (m' cos mu' - n' tanA cos nu') c' - (m' sin mu' - n' tanA sin nu') s'.
The page shows the first term on the right. Each side is an amplitude times a phase-shifted cosine, so the condition reads
A cos(psi+alpha) = A' cos(psi'+alpha').
A second such condition B cos(psi+beta) = B' cos(psi'+beta') is written beneath. In general one gets a relation of the form cos(psi'+const) = g cos(psi+const) + h, which can be substituted back to give a single equation in psi.
The scratch lines 'm cos mu - m' cos mu'.c, -m sin mu.s ..., -n tangA cos nu.c' are rough drafts of this collection of terms. The fragments 'M cos(psi+mu) = cos..., N cos(psi+nu) = sin...' and 'dd xi + ...' are too faint to reconstruct.

(4) Non-mathematical content (inverted text).
A list of candidate names: Neptun, Hebe, Flora, Latona, Proserpina, Iris, Cybele, Juno, Cupido, Pomona, Aesculap, Pluto. Planetary symbols accompany some of them: Neptune's trident, a cup-like sign near Hebe, flower-like signs near Flora, and a row of varied symbols.
The sideways text 'um neue Kronen zu gewinnen' and 'Numero' with symbols probably also concerns new planets and their symbols. Hencke asked Gauss to name the planet discovered in 1847, and Gauss chose Hebe, so this is plausibly Gauss's brainstorming of names and symbols in 1847.
errors: No mathematical error found in the visible expansion. The cc' coefficient -(m cos mu e' cos theta' - m' cos mu' e cos theta) is correct.

The page is fragmentary: the right-hand side of the circular-case equation shows only the c' term (the s' term is implicit), and the 'cos(psi'+..) = g cos(psi+..) + h' line has struck-out phase constants. These are incompleteness, not errors.
The derivation is not carried to the final elimination (quartic). That completion is mine.

results.what: Condition that the line joining two bodies on (possibly elliptic) orbits has prescribed direction A: tanA = (x-x')/(y-y'), with r = p/(1-e cos(psi+theta)) and coordinates in Gaussian constant form
results.modern_name: Relative/geocentric direction condition for two Keplerian orbits (e.g. finding when a planet has a given geocentric longitude)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-19th c. theoretical astronomy (Euler, Lagrange, Gauss's Theoria Motus 1809 for the coordinate constants)

results.what: Observation that after clearing denominators the equation is linear in (cos psi', sin psi') with coefficients linear in (1, cos psi, sin psi), allowing elimination via c'^2+s'^2=1 (quartic)
results.modern_name: Elimination of one angle from a bilinear trigonometric equation (resultant; quartic in half-angle tangent)

results.what: Circular-orbit reduction: condition becomes A cos(psi+alpha) = A' cos(psi'+alpha')
List of candidate names and symbols for newly discovered planets (Neptune, Hebe, Flora, Iris, ...), c. 1847
results.modern_name: Naming of asteroids (6 Hebe named by Gauss at Hencke's request)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss named Hebe (1847); other names by discoverers or other astronomers

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is routine celestial-mechanics algebra in Gauss's usual notation. The name list fits the known episode of Gauss naming Hebe in 1847; it is a nice archival detail but not a new result.
